...WINDY CONDITIONS FRIDAY...

Today: a trough digging south from the Gulf of Alaska will 
bring a southwest flow. Combined with higher heights linger over
the area, this will allow for mild day over the Upper Columbia 
Basin, Spokane Area, Palouse, and central Idaho areas with high 
in 70s and low 80s, roughly 10 degrees normal for this time of 
year. Elsewhere, temperatures will be near normal or slightly 
above normal. No precipitation is expected until late Thursday 
evening. 

Thursday night through Sunday: The offshore low continues to
deepen and a strong cold front will push across the Cascades 
late tonight into Friday morning, with the upper trough on its 
heels. The cold front is forecast to bring the rain, gusty 
winds, and chances for afternoon and evening thunderstorms. As 
with previous days before, there is still uncertainty around the
forecast details, particularly with winds and where the highest
wind gusts will occur. The deterministic ECMWF has higher wind 
gusts across a much broader area than the GFS, and the NBM 
75th-25th percentile spread for maximum gust speed is 10 mph 
throughout the entire forecast area. High-res models are finally
picking up on the bulk of the event, though, so we will 
continue monitoring the event closely in the next few forecast 
runs. 

A first area of precipitation associated with the cold front 
starts in the Cascades this evening. Chances expand into 
central WA overnight and early Friday, then into eastern WA and 
ID from mid-morning into early afternoon. At the same time, the 
incoming upper will bring second other scattered showers over 
the Cascades and central WA through the late morning to 
afternoon, which will then too migrates into eastern WA and 
north ID in the later afternoon to evening. Shower chances
linger around the mountain zones and perhaps far northeast WA
into the overnight, waning into Saturday. 

NBM probabilities show a 70 to 90 percent of at least 0.10 
inches of rain across the entire forecast area, save for the
deeper basin and L-C valley where rain probabilities are around
40-50%. Areas that will see the highest rainfall include the 
Cascades, northern mountains, Idaho Panhandle, which look to 
receive a third of an inch or more of rain and isolated rain 
totals up to 0.90 inches in the far northern mountains and 
Cascades. Snow amounts have stayed similar, with areas 6000-7000
feet and above in the Cascades having a chance to see a couple 
inches of snow. Elevations 5000 feet and above look to see under
an inch of snow. Any travelers or hikers anticipating being in 
those higher elevations this weekend should pay close attention 
to the forecast over the next few days. 

Cooling air aloft following the passage of the front support 
steep lapse rates (7 deg C/km and above), and SBCAPE values 
of 200 J/kg. Combined with the the upper trough forcing, there 
are chances for thunderstorms Friday afternoon and evening. 
Thunderstorm chances between 15-25% are found over the Cascades
through northern mountains, with a 10-15 percent chance over the
northern Columbia Basin into the Spokane area. Possible impacts
will be gusty outflow winds and isolated heavy rainfall.

Winds are shaping up to be the most notable part of the system. 
Winds increase with the cold frontal passage Friday, starting 
in the morning and peaking in the afternoon to evening (between
11 AM and 8 PM) before gradually waning into the overnight. 
Speeds have gotten progressively stronger with each model run. 
There remain model uncertainty regarding location and peak wind
strengthen. Regardless, NBM probabilities for peak wind gusts 
of 30 mph or greater average around 80 percent from the lee of
the Cascades to WA/ID border. For 40 mph or greater
probabilities are around 70-90% over the Waterville Plateau and
Upper Columbia Basin to the West Plains of Spokane. There is 
even 30-50% chance of wind gusts near 50 mph over the Upper 
Columbia Basin. Possible impacts include tree limb damage, 
airborne objects, difficulty driving especially for high profile
vehicles. Localized power outages could also be seen. Blowing 
dust will also be a potential from the lee of the Cascades to 
the West Plains of Spokane, south into the deeper Columbia Basin
in the afternoon and evening. This could lead to reduced 
visibilities.

Sunday through Tuesday: Temperatures remain slightly below 
normal into next week. Sunday and Monday morning may be chilly.
Lows in the low to mid 30s will be possible in sheltered 
northern valleys, which brings a frost threat. When looking at 
clusters, 80 percent agree on lower heights remaining over the 
area through Monday, though there is little agreement in 
strength and where the center of the low is. By Tuesday, 
confidence for continued lower heights decreases to 60 percent, 
overall indicating that unsettled weather may continue into next
week. Overall the forecast looks drier, save for some periods
mountain shower chances. /AS/Solveig
